lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flávio Masaharu Kuroda | Lesson 11 -- Say That Again
lesson.grammar_point: checking questions and paraphrase for clarification

listenings.text: When people do not understand something on a call, most of them do one of two things. They nod and hope it becomes clear later, or they apologize for their English and ask the other person to repeat everything. Both of those are expensive. The first one creates a misunderstanding that you discover three weeks later, in the contract. The second one sends the whole conversation back to the beginning, and it tells everybody on the call that the problem is you. There is a third option, and it is the one good negotiators use even in their own language. You repeat the part you did catch, and you ask only for the missing piece. Did you say March or May? What does that acronym stand for? So you mean the pilot is paid? One short question, and the call keeps moving. Nobody hears a problem. They hear somebody who is paying attention.

I work with partners in eleven countries, and English is the first language of almost none of us. What I have learned is that the people who ask the most questions on a call are usually the people I trust the most afterwards. When somebody stops me and says, so what you are saying is that the data stays in Germany, I know two things. I know they were listening, and I know that if they understood it wrong, I can correct it now, in ten seconds, instead of in a meeting with lawyers. The people who worry me are the ones who never ask anything. Every sentence is fine, perfect, understood. And then the proposal arrives, and it is clear that they understood the gist but not the details. I would much rather spell something out twice than discover later that we were talking about two different projects.
